summary: The US disables a ship leaving Iran, Earth logs a record run of days above 2C, Venezuela moves to scrap a ban on opponents, and Serbia's students pick a presidential candidate.

topics.heading: US strikes a cargo ship leaving Iran; Tehran vows to break the blockade
topics.summary: US Central Command says an aircraft disabled the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman after it left an Iranian port, with no crew hurt.[^1][^2] An adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader says Iran will not accept the blockade, without saying how it would act.[^1]

lead.title: US disables ship trying to leave Iran, as Tehran vows to confront blockade

alsoReported.title: US Disables Palau-Flagged Cargo Ship Attempting to Break Iran Blockade

article: Since July the United States has blockaded Iran's ports, stopping ships from entering or leaving, as part of the war that began in February.[^1] On Thursday, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which runs US forces in the Middle East, said one of its aircraft struck the stern of the Pacific Archer, a bulk carrier flagged in Palau, after it sailed from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The strike knocked out the ship's engines; CENTCOM says the civilian crew was unharmed.[^1][^2]

CENTCOM says the crew ignored repeated warnings. It also says US forces have redirected 158 commercial ships that obeyed its orders and disabled six whose crews refused.[^2] These figures come from the US military alone, and the outlets reporting them did not check them independently.

Iran's answer was defiant. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, told Iranian state media that the Strait of Hormuz would not be reopened "nor will we allow the blockade to remain in place".[^1] He did not say what Iran would do. Earlier this month the US also set up Task Force Iron Gate to restrict weapons and sanctioned goods crossing Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.[^1]
Why it matters: each side is squeezing the other's trade. The US blockade cuts Iran's oil income, while Iran's pressure on Hormuz keeps shipping and oil prices unsettled for everyone else.
My read: this is a slow contest of endurance rather than a turn toward a deal. Watch for any Iranian move against US ships or the escort corridors, and for any sign that talks restart.
topics.differences: CENTCOM says the Pacific Archer tried to run the blockade despite warnings.[^2] Iran's leadership calls the blockade illegitimate and says it will not let it stand.[^1] No independent account of the incident has been published.

topics.heading: Earth's daily temperature stays more than 2C above pre-industrial for a record run
topics.summary: Preliminary Copernicus data show global surface temperature above 2C over the 1850-1900 average for six or seven days in a row, a first.[^3][^4] Scientists stress this is not a breach of the Paris goals, which use long-term averages.[^3][^4]

lead.title: World breaches 2C temperature limit six days in a row for first time

alsoReported.title: Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time

article: Copernicus, the EU's climate monitoring service, tracks global surface temperature every day. Its preliminary data show the planet stayed more than 2C warmer than the 1850-1900 average for at least six days in a row, a run never seen before. The peak came on November 23, at about 2.24C to 2.25C, the largest daily gap on record.[^3][^4] Before this, days above 2C had been rare: two in November 2023 and four in February 2024.[^4]

A key point: the Paris Agreement's limits of 1.5C and 2C refer to averages over many years, not single days, so this streak does not mean the limits are broken.[^3][^4] Copernicus puts the long-term warming level at about 1.44C.[^3]

Two things are adding together. The main cause is the build-up of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels. On top of that, a strong El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, is releasing extra heat.[^3] Samantha Burgess of Copernicus called the streak "a clear preview of where our climate is heading" and noted that El Niño is temporary while the underlying warming stays.[^4] Zachary Labe of Climate Central expects more days above 2C through about March 2027, though still "more a rarity than the norm".[^3]

The timing is awkward for diplomacy. The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on November 22 without its main political agreement after disputes over fossil fuels and money, though a few smaller decisions passed.[^4][^5]

What next: Copernicus says 2026 will very likely be the second-warmest year on record, and its director sees a fairly high chance of at least one full year above 2C before 2030.[^4] My read: the daily records are a warning sign, not the threshold itself.
topics.differences: The Independent counts six consecutive days and a peak of 2.24C; MercoPress, citing Copernicus a day later, counts seven days and 2.25C. The gap reflects different cut-off dates and preliminary data.[^3][^4]

topics.heading: Venezuela moves to repeal the law used to bar opponents from office
topics.summary: National Assembly chief Jorge Rodríguez says Venezuela will repeal a 2024 law that bans people who backed foreign sanctions from public office.[^6][^7] Opposition leader María Corina Machado, back from exile, has started nationwide neighbourhood meetings.[^6]

lead.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office

alsoReported.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office

article: Venezuela is in a political transition. Since US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro in January, an interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez has run the country, and it has held talks with parts of the opposition chosen with Washington's backing.[^6] Those talks agreed to review several laws, including one passed after the disputed July 2024 election.[^6][^7]

That law, often called the Simón Bolívar Law, permanently banned anyone who asked for or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela from holding office and allowed their assets to be seized.[^7] Critics said it was a tool for political persecution. On Thursday, Jorge Rodríguez, the head of the National Assembly and Delcy Rodríguez's brother, said it "responded to a very specific moment" and would be repealed.[^6][^7] He told the BBC no politician had actually been punished under it and expects approval next week.[^7]

The repeal matters for María Corina Machado, who won the 2023 opposition primary but was barred from running in 2024. She returned from exile in October and is widely expected to run if an election is called, though she was left out of the transition talks.[^6][^7] On Thursday her team launched neighbourhood assemblies asking people 19 questions about election dates, wages, pensions and public services; it says about 2,000 meetings were held on the first day.[^6]

What next: Delcy Rodríguez promised free and fair elections at the UN in September but has set no date.[^6] My read: removing the ban is a real step, but the test is whether a date is set and opponents can campaign freely.
topics.differences: The interim government says the law fitted a past moment and was never actually used against a politician.[^7] The opposition and critics say it was designed to keep opponents out of politics, and Venezuela's opposition still says it won the 2024 election.[^6][^7]

topics.heading: Russia hits Ukraine's power grid with 155 drones as Ukraine strikes Russian plants
topics.summary: Ukraine's military says Russia launched 155 drones overnight and 110 were stopped; power went out in six regions.[^8][^9] Ukraine says it struck a Russian chemical plant tied to missile fuel, while Russian officials report drones over St Petersburg.[^9]

lead.title: Russian attacks kill 6, injure 25 across Ukraine over past day, power outages across 6 oblasts

alsoReported.title: Russian drone strikes hit Ukraine's energy, rail and civilian infrastructure, causing deaths

article: For more than a year, Russia and Ukraine have attacked each other's energy systems, and winter raises the stakes because people need heat and light. Overnight into Friday, Ukrainian officials said Russia launched 155 drones, including jet-powered ones and decoys, and that 110 were shot down or jammed.[^8] Ukraine's first deputy energy minister, Artem Nekrasov, said strikes on substations cut power in six regions, with Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson worst hit.[^8][^9]

Ukrainian regional officials reported six people killed and 25 injured over the previous day, including an 86-year-old woman in the Kharkiv region.[^8] Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky said railways, energy sites, businesses and homes in nine regions were hit.[^9] Euronews, citing the Centre for Economic Strategy, a Kyiv think tank, says Ukraine has stopped exporting electricity since a November 20 attack and is importing more.[^9]

Ukraine struck back. Its General Staff says drones hit a synthetic rubber plant in Yefremov, south of Moscow, that it says makes parts for solid rocket fuel used in Iskander missiles.[^9] St Petersburg officials said they downed 45 drones, and Russia's defence ministry claimed 318 Ukrainian drones were shot down across Russia and Crimea.[^9] President Zelenskyy said Ukraine is "absolutely right" to respond to every Russian strike.[^9]

My read: neither side is close to knocking out the other's energy system, but both are raising the cost of winter. Watch whether talk of a US-brokered energy truce returns, and whether Ukraine's power imports keep rising.
topics.differences: Ukraine and Russia each report how many of the other's drones they shot down; neither set of figures has been independently checked, and they are not comparable.[^8][^9]

topics.heading: Serbia's student movement names a chemistry professor for the Dec. 27 presidential vote
topics.summary: The Students List, which beat Aleksandar Vučić's party in October, picked professor Radomir Saičić as its presidential candidate.[^10][^11] Vučić has suggested his party may boycott the vote.[^10][^11]

lead.title: Serbia's student movement proposes a chemistry professor for presidency ahead of Dec. 27 ballot

alsoReported.title: Serbia's student-led movement nominates chemistry professor for presidency

article: Serbia's protests began in November 2024, when a concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station collapsed and killed 16 people. Many Serbians blamed corruption, and students led the largest demonstrations since the fall of Slobodan Milošević in 2000.[^10][^11] Their movement, the Students List, won the October 25 parliamentary election, taking 140 of 250 seats and defeating the governing SNS party.[^11]

Aleksandar Vučić had dominated Serbian politics for 14 years. He resigned the presidency in September to run for prime minister, lost, and is now an opposition MP; the constitution bars him from running for president again.[^10][^11] That left an early presidential vote on December 27.

On Friday the movement named Radomir Saičić, 65, an organic chemistry professor at the University of Belgrade and member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts.[^10] He said the last decade was marred by the crumbling of the rule of law, corruption and hate speech, and that parliament, government and courts must earn back public trust.[^10][^11]

The presidency is mostly ceremonial, but the president nominates prime ministers and commands the army.[^11] Analysts expect the student candidate to win. Vučić has accused the new majority of "revolutionary terror" as officials suspected of abusing their posts are detained, and has hinted the SNS may sit out the vote; a decision is expected in mid-December.[^10][^11]
My read: a student-backed president would complete a rare peaceful change of power. Watch whether the SNS takes part, which will shape how legitimate the result looks to its voters.
topics.differences: Saičić and the students say they are restoring the rule of law.[^10] Vučić says the new majority is carrying out "revolutionary terror" against officials.[^10]

question.text: Venezuela and Serbia are both being described as moving toward democracy. What are we assuming when we use that label, and what would you need to see over the next year before you believed it?

read.title: World breaches 2C temperature limit six days in a row for first time
read.summary: A clear explainer of the record 2C streak: what the numbers mean, why a few hot days are not a Paris breach, and how El Niño and greenhouse gases add up.
